title: Three-quarters of adults in Great Britain worry about climate change
meta_description: Article about public attitudes and opinions towards climate change and the future of the environment.

breadcrumb.text: Measuring progress, well-being and beyond GDP
Three-quarters of adults in Great Britain worry about climate change

lede: Those who are worried about climate change are also more likely to make lifestyle changes in response.

body.text: 5 November 2021

In October 2021, just ahead of the COP26 UN Climate conference in Glasgow, three-quarters (75%) of adults in Great Britain said they were worried about the impact of climate change, [according to the Office for National Statistics’ (ONS’) Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN).](/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/datasets/dataonpublicattitudestotheenvironmentandtheimpactofclimatechangegreatbritain)
Just over two-fifths (43%) reported feeling anxious about the future of the environment more widely in the past month.
Women were more likely to report worry about both the impact of climate change and anxiety about the future of the environment than men.

Adults who reported being worried about the impact of climate change were three times more likely to have made a lot of changes to their lifestyle in response to the issue than those who were relatively unworried.
In the survey, people were also asked to describe in their own words how they feel about the future of the environment. Some common themes were identified in the responses, such as:
people’s concern for their family and future generations
anxiety and helplessness
the expense of making eco-friendly changes.

body.h3: “[I’m] concerned for what we are leaving our younger generation to cope with.”
body.text: “[I’m] concerned for what we are leaving our younger generation to cope with.”

body.h3: “[I’m] concerned for what we are leaving our younger generation to cope with.”
body.text: In October 2021, three-quarters (75%) of adults in Great Britain said they were either very or somewhat worried about the impact of climate change, while around one-fifth (19%) were neither worried nor unworried.

body.h3: “[I’m] concerned for what we are leaving our younger generation to cope with.”
body.text: Around 8 in 10 women (79%) reported being either very or somewhat worried. This was statistically significantly higher than the proportion of men reporting this (72%).

body.h3: “[I’m] concerned for what we are leaving our younger generation to cope with.”
body.text: Those aged 70 years and over were less likely to report that they were very worried than some younger age groups. Just under a quarter (24%) of those aged 70 years and over reported being very worried compared with 37% of those aged 25 to 34 years and 34% of those aged 35 to 49 years. For those reporting some level of worry (either very or somewhat worried) there was no significant difference between age groups.

body.text: The proportion of adults reporting some level of worry was similar across Great Britain. It was 75% for both England and Wales and 74% in Scotland. Within England, adults in London appeared slightly more likely to report being either very or somewhat worried.

body.h3: “[I’m] concerned for what we are leaving our younger generation to cope with.”
body.h4: Women were more likely than men to be worried about the impact of climate change
body.text: These findings for Great Britain are similar to results of [the Department of Business Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) Public Attitudes Tracker](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/beis-public-attitudes-tracker-wave-33) which surveys UK households. In March 2020, this found that around three-quarters (76%) of adults in the UK were concerned to some degree about climate change. [The Northern Ireland statistics and research agency (NISRA) survey (PDF, 2.5MB) found](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/daera/ni-environmental-statistics-report-2021.pdf) that in 2019 to 2020, 78% of adults reported being very or fairly concerned about the environment; there was no question specifically on concern about climate change.

body.h3: “I'm fearful for my family's future.”
body.text: “I'm fearful for my family's future.”

body.h3: “I'm fearful for my family's future.”
body.text: In free-text responses about how they felt about the future of the environment, a common theme was worry for family, and worry for future generations.

body.h3: “I'm fearful for my family's future.”
body.text: However, some people were worried about the impacts of efforts to combat climate change, such as expressing concern that any effort “creates more problems than it solves”.

body.h3: “I'm fearful for my family's future.”
body.text: Themes identified in the free-text responses largely reflected negative emotions such as worry, frustration and alarm. However, as the free-text questions were optional, it may be that some were more likely to respond to these than others, so the quotes used are not illustrative of the whole population.

body.text: Adults in younger age groups appeared to be more likely to report feeling not at all anxious, compared with older age groups. Among those aged 16 to 24 years, 22% reported being not at all anxious compared with 9% among those aged 70 years and over.

body.text: The survey also asked about how positive or negative people felt about the future of the environment. Nearly two-thirds (63%) reported feeling somewhat or very negative when they thought about the future of the environment. Again, this appeared slightly more common in younger age groups (67% of those aged 16 to 24 years, 67% of those aged 25 to 34 years, 68% of those aged 35 to 49 years) than in older age groups (61% of those aged 65 to 69 years, 55% of those aged 70 years and above).

body.h3: "I think the future is pretty bleak as so much damage has already been done.”
body.h4: Younger age groups appeared slightly more likely to report being very anxious about the future of the environment
body.text: Despite these levels of worry and negative feeling about the future of the environment, some respondents did express optimism in the free-text responses. These more positive comments tended to reference global commitment, investment, and progress as reasons for feeling more upbeat about the future, such as: “I think we are taking strides to have a more green future with the introduction of electric cars etc”.

body.text: Overall, 81% of adults in Great Britain reported having made some or a lot of lifestyle changes to help tackle climate change.

body.h3: "I feel dread, anxiousness and hopelessness. Then I feel energised to do something."
body.text: One in eight of those who reported some level of worry (12%) said they had made a lot of lifestyle changes, compared with 4% of those who were relatively unworried.

body.h3: "I feel dread, anxiousness and hopelessness. Then I feel energised to do something."
body.text: Of adults who reported some level of worry, 9 in 10 (90%) said they had made some or a lot of changes to their lifestyle. This compares with 55% of those who were relatively unworried and 52% of those who were neither worried nor unworried.

body.text: Adults in the oldest and youngest age groups appeared slightly less likely to report having made lifestyle changes (74% of those aged 70 years and over and 77% of those aged 16 to 24 years). Around 8 in 10 of those in other age groups reported this (80% of those aged 25 to 34 years, 85% of those aged 35 to 49 years, and 84% of those aged 50 to 69 years).

body.h3: "I feel dread, anxiousness and hopelessness. Then I feel energised to do something."
body.h4: Those worried about the impact of climate change were more likely to make lifestyle changes to help tackle it
body.text: Around 8 in 10 people (82%) agreed that if everyone did their bit, we could reduce the effects of climate change, according to similar survey data from BEIS. In March 2020, 83% of people reported at least one environmentally friendly adaptation to their lifestyle, with the most common being avoiding or minimising throwing away food. However, only around a quarter of those who minimised throwing away food (26%) did so to tackle climate change. Two-thirds (66%) did so for mainly for other reasons, such as lifestyle choice, cost, convenience, health, or ethical reasons.

body.h3: “The planet was here long before us and it will be here long after.”
body.text: “The planet was here long before us and it will be here long after.”

body.h3: “The planet was here long before us and it will be here long after.”
body.text: Of the quarter (25%) of adults who reported to the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN) in October 2021 that they were relatively unworried or ambivalent (not at all worried, somewhat unworried or neither worried nor unworried) about the impacts of climate change, the most common reasons for this were not knowing much about the issue (35%) or thinking there are other more urgent priorities to be worried about (34%).

body.h3: “The planet was here long before us and it will be here long after.”
body.text: Among adults in younger age groups who were relatively unworried or ambivalent about climate change, the most common reason was not knowing much about climate change (62% of those aged 16 to 24 years and 49% of those aged 25 to 34 years). Younger adults were also less likely to report thinking that there were other more urgent priorities to worry about (28% of those aged 16 to 24 years and 27% of those aged 25 to 34 years).

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN)
body.text: This release contains data and indicators from the Office for National Statistics' (ONS') Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN). Data presented in this article were collected between 6 and 17 October 2021, with respondents aged 16 years and over in Great Britain.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN)
body.text: Breakdowns by age, sex, region and country, including [confidence intervals](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/methodologytopicsandstatisticalconcepts/uncertaintyandhowwemeasureit#confidence-interval) for the estimates, are contained in the accompanying dataset.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN)
body.text: Where differences in estimates are presented in this bulletin, associated confidence intervals have been used to assess the [statistical significance](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/methodologytopicsandstatisticalconcepts/uncertaintyandhowwemeasureit#statistical-significance) of these differences.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN)
body.text: In this period, between 6 and 17 October, we sampled 5,901 households. These were randomly selected from those that had previously completed the Labour Market Survey (LMS) or OPN. The responding sample contained 4,004 individuals, representing a 68% response rate.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN)
body.text: Survey weights were applied to make estimates representative of the population (based on September 2021 population estimates). Further information on the survey design and quality can be found in [the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey QMI.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/methodologies/opinionsandlifestylesurveyqmi)

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Free-text responses
body.text: Free-text responses

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Free-text responses
body.text: Survey respondents were asked; ‘In a few words, please describe how you feel when you think about the future of the environment’.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Free-text responses
body.text: Free-text responses were analysed using a natural language processing method by Christopher Collins in the Methodology, Census and Population Statistics Hub in the ONS. The processing identified similar responses and grouped them together into themes.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Free-text responses
body.text: The natural language processing output was then reviewed for accuracy and responses grouped thematically, selecting quotes from a broad range of participants to illustrate each theme. We then undertook a full quality assurance review of the analysis to ensure the quotes selected were an impartial representation of each theme.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: Free-text responses
body.text: Quotes have been used throughout the article to represent the notable themes identified in the analysis. All survey responses were anonymous and any potentially identifying information has been removed from the quotes.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: BEIS Public Attitudes Tracker
body.text: This article includes data from [the Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) Public Attitudes Tracker.](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/beis-public-attitudes-tracker-wave-33) Findings are based on the 33rd wave collected between 11 and 17 March 2020, conducted using face-to-face in-home interviews with a representative sample of 1,850 households in the UK.

body.h3: Measuring the data
body.h4: BEIS Public Attitudes Tracker
body.text: Face-to-face fieldwork was suspended in March 2020. Data for the second half of wave 33 and subsequent waves (34 to 37) were collected from an online omnibus panel. Because of selection and measurement effects, for comparison purposes, this report uses data from the latest face-to-face survey rather than from the online panel survey conducted between June 2020 and March 2021. Further information about the survey’s methods is available on the BEIS Public Attitudes Tracker website.

body.text: Supporting data on attitudes in Northern Ireland in this article were sourced from Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency Continuous Household Survey data used within the [Northern Ireland Environmental Statistics Report 2021](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/publications/northern-ireland-environmental-statistics-report-2021). Following the start of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, face-to-face fieldwork was suspended for this survey. For comparison purposes, data collected from before the suspension have been used in this article. Full information on data quality and methods are presented in [the report’s user guide (PDF, 797KB)](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/daera/ni-environmental-statistics-report-user-guidance-2021.pdf).
